title: The Elasticity of Taxable Income: Evidence and Implications
research_question: How responsive is reported taxable income to changes in marginal tax rates, and does this responsiveness vary across the income distribution? Additionally, what are the relative magnitudes of substitution and income effects in determining how individuals adjust their reported income when tax rates change, and how does the responsiveness of a broad measure of real income compare to that of taxable income?
data_description: The analysis uses the NBER panel of individual federal tax returns (the Continuous Work History File) covering tax years 1979 through 1990. The panel is constructed by selecting taxpayers based on specified four-digit endings of the primary filer's Social Security number, with sample sizes varying by year (approximately 46,000 observations in 1979–1981 and smaller in subsequent years). The unit of observation is the individual tax return (taxpayer-year). Key variables drawn from Form 1040 and associated schedules include wages, interest, dividends, business income, pensions, partnership income, itemized deductions, exemptions, marital status, and filing status. Two income concepts are constructed consistently across years: 'broad income' (a comprehensive gross income measure excluding capital gains and Social Security benefits) and 'taxable income' (broad income net of exemptions and deductions, fixed at 1990 definitions). Federal and state marginal tax rates and tax liabilities are computed using the NBER TAXSIM calculator. Observations with base-year broad income below $10,000 and those with marital status changes are excluded.
institutional_context: The 1980s in the United States featured a dramatic restructuring of the federal personal income tax. The Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (ERTA) phased in across-the-board rate cuts from 1982 to 1984, lowering the top marginal rate from 70% to 50%. The Tax Reform Act of 1986 (TRA86) further compressed the rate schedule into four brackets and reduced the top rate to 28%, while broadening the base by raising the standard deduction and personal exemptions. The Earned Income Tax Credit was substantially expanded in 1987. In addition, numerous state income tax systems underwent independent reforms during this decade, with many states cutting their top rates and reducing the number of brackets (e.g., New York, Minnesota, Delaware), while a few states raised rates. Bracket creep before indexation (pre-1985) also generated mechanical changes in marginal rates. Together, these federal and state changes produced rich variation in marginal tax rates that differed across income groups, states, and years.
